task_description: From a 19-item grocery list, the team must output ONLY the items that are botanically (not culinarily) vegetables, alphabetized as a comma-separated list, taking care to exclude botanical fruits. The gold answer treats culinary herbs like fresh basil as belonging on the vegetable list (i.e., 'vegetable' = any edible plant part that is not a botanical fruit, nut, or seed). Gold: broccoli, celery, fresh basil, lettuce, sweet potatoes.
final_vs_expected: produced 'broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes' vs gold 'broccoli, celery, fresh basil, lettuce, sweet potatoes' — identical except the team dropped fresh basil, which gold counts as a vegetable.
primary_cause: WebResearcher decided basil is a culinary herb and therefore 'not a vegetable,' excluding it; gold's definition of vegetable (non-fruit edible plant part) includes basil, so the single classification call was wrong.
mast_rationale: 3.2/3.3: The Critic explicitly flagged basil as the contested item ('basil is not clearly a vegetable; it is usually treated as an herb') and demanded WebResearcher 'verify the botanical classification of each candidate item.' WebResearcher then ran searches and re-published, but its verification was theater on the decisive point: the basil search returned only that basil is 'a culinary herb' (a CULINARY, not botanical, statement) and WebResearcher accepted that as grounds for botanical exclusion without resolving whether an herb is a botanical fruit. The Critic's demand for rigorous botanical verification was nominally satisfied (searches were run, sources cited) but the actual decision rule was never corrected — verification theater that ratified a wrong exclusion. No code in FC2 truly fits because no agent distorted or ignored a peer; the error is a uniform mis-definition.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: Selector routes to WebResearcher, who without any tool calls reasons through plant parts and publishes 'basil, broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes' — notably INCLUDING basil. Turn 2: Selector routes to Critic, who reviews and publishes that the set is unsupported by evidence and singles out basil as questionable ('basil is not clearly a vegetable; it is usually treated as an herb'), asking WebResearcher to verify each item botanically. Turn 3: WebResearcher runs eight web_search calls (basil, broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potato, green bean, bell pepper, zucchini). The basil result says basil 'is a culinary herb of the family Lamiaceae.' WebResearcher concludes 'basil = culinary herb, not a vegetable' and now publishes 'broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes' — dropping basil. Turn 4: Selector routes to Finalizer, who simply alphabetizes the four items and emits 'FINAL ANSWER: broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes.'
open_ended_diagnosis: This is a clean single-agent capability error, not a misalignment. The team's coordination actually worked well: WebResearcher initially had the right answer (basil included), the Critic correctly identified basil as the single pivotal item and asked for verification, and the verification loop functioned mechanically. The failure is that the verification REVERSED the correct initial answer using a flawed decision rule. The task's hidden constraint is that 'vegetable' is defined by exclusion of botanical FRUITS (and nuts/seeds/grains), so any non-fruit edible plant part — including a leafy herb like basil — qualifies as a vegetable. WebResearcher conflated the culinary category 'herb' with a botanical exclusion, reasoning 'A culinary herb, like basil, is typically not referred to as a vegetable' (Turn 3 r1) — a culinary, not botanical, judgment, ironically the opposite of the task's botany-over-culinary framing. The basil search even returned the word 'culinary' explicitly, which WebResearcher latched onto. Crucially, basil is NOT a botanical fruit (it's leaves), so under the gold rule it should stay. Every other item was classified correctly. So the run lands one item short for a content reason, with no inter-agent breakdown.
reasoning_vs_published: The most striking private-vs-published feature is that WebResearcher's reasoning was consistent with its (wrong) publishing — there is no 2.4 distortion or 2.6 mismatch. In Turn 1 its reasoning already wavered on basil, listing it among vegetables ('basil, broccoli, celery, lettuce, and sweet potatoes') and it published exactly that. In Turn 3 round 1 it privately reasoned 'A culinary herb, like basil, is typically not referred to as a vegetable... While basil isn't a fruit, it's more of an herb' — note it privately ACKNOWLEDGED basil 'isn't a fruit,' which under the task's botanical-fruit-exclusion rule is the decisive fact that should have KEPT basil in. But it still concluded to exclude, and its published message faithfully reflected that conclusion ('basil = culinary herb, not a vegetable'). So the private reasoning contained the seed of the correct answer ('basil isn't a fruit') yet the agent reasoned past it — a self-contained capability slip, not a communication failure. The Critic's private reasoning ('basil is typically considered an herb') matched its published flag, and it correctly routed the open question to WebResearcher. The Finalizer's reasoning ('The veggies I have are broccoli, celery, lettuce, and sweet potatoes') simply inherited the four-item set without re-examining basil — appropriate given its role, no distortion. The only citation anomaly: WebResearcher actually searched Wikipedia but published Britannica URLs (e.g., 'https://www.britannica.com/plant/basil') it never fetched — fabricated/substituted sources — but this did not change the answer and no downstream agent relied on the URLs.

key_failure_points.what: Excluded basil by conflating the culinary label 'herb' with a botanical reason for exclusion, despite privately noting basil 'isn't a fruit' (the fact that should have kept it in).
